summary.text: Electromagnetic radiation is a self-propagating wave of the electromagnetic field that carries momentum and radiant energy through space.
It covers a spectrum sorted by frequency, from radio waves through visible light to X-rays and gamma rays, and every kind travels at the speed of light in a vacuum.
It is produced by accelerating charged particles, and it behaves both as a wave and as particles called photons.

facts.label: The spectrum
facts.value: Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, UV, X-rays, gamma rays

facts.label: Wave shape
facts.value: Transverse in uniform media, oscillating sideways to its travel

facts.label: Dual nature
facts.value: Acts as both a wave and as photons

items.prompt: Sunlight reaches Earth after crossing millions of kilometres of empty space. Why is that possible?

options.label: Its energy travels along a thin trail of dust
Its energy needs no medium to move through
It slows to a crawl until it meets air
Space carries it like waves carry a boat

items.explain: The energy of electromagnetic waves does not need a propagating medium; they move through a vacuum at the speed of light.

items.prompt: White sunlight passes through a glass prism and fans out into colours. What causes the fan-out?

options.label: The prism adds colour that was not in the light
The prism heats some parts of the light more
The prism filters out all but one wavelength
Each wavelength is bent a different amount

items.explain: The prism material's refractive index depends on wavelength, so each component of the mixed light bends by a different amount.

items.prompt: A charged particle sits at rest and is then pushed so that it speeds up. What can result?

options.label: It can give off electromagnetic radiation
It becomes neutral at once
It absorbs all light around it
It stops interacting with fields

items.explain: Electromagnetic radiation is produced by accelerating charged particles.

items.prompt: Think of a light wave as a ripple in electric and magnetic fields. How do those wiggles lie compared with the direction the wave travels?

options.label: Along the same line as the travel direction
Perpendicular to the direction of travel
Spiralling backward against the travel
Only up and down, never sideways

items.explain: In uniform media the radiation is a transverse wave, with oscillations perpendicular to the direction of energy travel.

items.prompt: Very dim light goes through a device and each detection happens along only one path, yet many detections together form a striped pattern. What does this show?

options.label: The detector is faulty
Light only ever acts as a stream of particles
Light shows both particle and wave behaviour
Light only ever acts as a smooth wave

items.explain: Single detections fit particle properties, while the accumulated interference fits wave properties: wave-particle duality.

items.prompt: Radio waves and X-rays are both electromagnetic radiation, yet X-rays call for more care. Why?

options.label: X-rays travel faster than radio waves
X-rays need a material medium to carry them
X-rays are produced only by large machines
Higher-energy radiation is linked to health harm

items.explain: Higher-energy radiation, especially UV and above, is associated with negative health effects, though X-rays are also applied in medical imaging.

paragraphs.heading: A wave that carries itself
paragraphs.text: Electromagnetic radiation is a wave in the electromagnetic field that keeps itself going as it travels, carrying energy and momentum through space. The energy it carries is sometimes called radiant energy. It needs no material to move through: it crosses empty space at the speed of light. Every kind of this radiation travels at that same speed in a vacuum.

paragraphs.heading: One family, many kinds
paragraphs.text: The radiation comes in a wide range, sorted by frequency; the higher the frequency, the shorter the wavelength. The range runs from radio waves and microwaves through infrared, visible light and ultraviolet to X-rays and gamma rays. Frequency is how fast the wave oscillates, counted in hertz, where one hertz means one oscillation each second. How the radiation acts on matter depends on its wavelength, and that shapes how each kind is used.

paragraphs.heading: What we use it for
paragraphs.text: Radio waves carry broadcasts and wireless signals, infrared makes thermal imaging possible, and visible light is what lets us see. The higher-energy kinds, X-rays and gamma rays, help doctors image the body and treat cancer, and help industry inspect parts. Radiation from ultraviolet upward has also been linked with harm to health.

paragraphs.heading: Where it comes from
paragraphs.text: The radiation is produced by charged particles that accelerate. Some is natural, pouring out of the Sun and other objects in space, and some is made by people for their own purposes. Quantum effects add further sources, such as an electron in an atom dropping to a lower energy level, and black-body radiation.

paragraphs.heading: How the wave is built
paragraphs.text: In a uniform material that behaves the same in every direction, the wave is transverse: its fields swing at right angles to the way it travels. Its electric and magnetic parts keep a fixed ratio of strength, as two of Maxwell's equations demand, since those equations say how each field produces the other. In a material that loses no energy, the two fields also rise and fall in step. When a wave passes into a different material, its speed changes but its frequency does not.

paragraphs.heading: Bending and splitting light
paragraphs.text: When a wave crosses into a material of different density, it changes speed and direction; this is refraction. How much it bends is set by the ratio of the two materials' refractive indices, a rule known as Snell's law. A prism bends each wavelength by a different amount, so sunlight passing through it fans out into a visible spectrum. This spreading of frequencies is called dispersion.

paragraphs.heading: Wave and particle at once
paragraphs.text: The radiation also behaves as particles called photons, which carry no charge and have zero rest mass. Its wave side shows up when it is measured over long times and distances, and its particle side over short ones. A single photon can even interfere with itself. Send very dim light through an interferometer and a sensitive detector catches each arrival in just one arm of the device, like a particle, yet many arrivals add up to an interference pattern, like a wave.
